I have a summer project student, @Merle In der Rieden , and we're going to try and put a Riemannian metric on the n-sphere (which will be a lot of fun for me because I have a very shaky understanding of manifolds).

We've got as far as something which typechecks, but I've been reading all the small print and I am now fairly confident that I've asked Merle to do something impossible.

import Mathlib.Geometry.Manifold.Riemannian.Basic
import Mathlib.Geometry.Manifold.Instances.Sphere

open Module Metric

open scoped Manifold

variable {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]

variable {n : ℕ} [Fact (finrank ℝ E = n + 1)]

instance : Bundle.RiemannianBundle fun (x : sphere (0 : E) 1) ↦ TangentSpace (𝓡 n) x := sorry

instance : IsRiemannianManifold (𝓡 n) (sphere (0 : E) 1) := by
  sorry

#synth EMetricSpace (sphere (0 : E) 1) -- oops

It seems that a Riemannian manifold comes with a specified metric which presumably is supposed to be the metric induced by the Riemannian structure. However, if EEE is an inner product space, then sphere (0 : E) 1 (coerced to a type), the type which Heather put a manifold structure on, already has a metric space structure, coming from the metric space structure on EEE and docs#instEMetricSpaceSubtype . This presumably is not the right metric, as it will allow travelling through the sphere.

Any advice?
(I'll try to respond to this very soon, but need to run now - first teaching, then an important meeting.)

You are absolutely right that the distance coming from being a subset is not the geodesic distance. When you say that you're trying to put a Riemannian metric, do you mean just an inner product structure on all the tangent spaces that varies smoothly with the point, or do you mean also the associated distance on the sphere? If it's the former, there is nothing special to do, just define it and prove what you have to prove. If it's the latter, you should use a type synonym.
(if you go for a type synonym, you should probably call it RoundSphere)
(Or GeodesicSphere ?)

I meant an instance of docs#IsRiemannianManifold . Ok, RoundSphere/GeodesicSphere it is. But I thought type synonyms were banned nowadays? Should we make it a one field structure? If so, do we have a way of pulling back manifold structures along bijections?

RoundSphere is really the standard name in the literature (see e.g. https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/round+sphere).

Type synonyms are absolutely not banned. Quite the opposite, they work much better with recent Lean versions. Just use deriving to get the manifold structure.

The construction I have as a PR gives you a Riemannian metric on any (finite dimensional) manifold. I am pretty sure that it will give the round sphere when applied to the sphere: https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/33714

This may be an answer

As the Mathlib documentation states (Mathlib.Analysis.Normed.Module.FiniteDimension):

"The fact that all norms are equivalent is not written explicitly, as it would mean having
two norms on a single space, which is not the way type classes work. However, if one has a
finite-dimensional vector space E with a norm, and a copy E' of this type with another
norm, then the identities from E to E' and from E' to E are continuous thanks to
LinearMap.continuous_of_finiteDimensional. This gives the desired norm equivalence."
(https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Module/FiniteDimension.html)

It is well known that all norms on a finite-dimensional space are equivalent.
In Mathlib, making this work requires explicit construction and proof. -/

I'm back on this. I'm having trouble with the type synonym:

import Mathlib.Geometry.Manifold.Riemannian.Basic
import Mathlib.Geometry.Manifold.Instances.Sphere

variable (E : Type*) [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]

open Metric

#synth EMetricSpace (sphere (0 : E) 1) -- works :-)

def RoundSphere := sphere (0 : E) 1

#synth EMetricSpace (RoundSphere E) -- works :-(

Is a one-field structure the only way to continue?
Your RoundSphere is a Set E, but you should make it a Type _ if you want to declare new instances on it.

Here's an update.

I've had a summer student working on putting a Riemannian metric on the n-sphere and the project finished today. We have something working locally. I learnt a lot about how mathlib does manifolds, so this has been very illuminating for me! After some initial experiments we followed Sébastien's path explained here #maths > Is this a manifold? @ 💬 to the construction. I have some mathlib-related questions.

1) (I've brought this up before). The n-sphere already has a manifold structure:

import Mathlib.Geometry.Manifold.Instances.Sphere

open Metric Module Function Manifold

variable (E : Type*) [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]
  (n : ℕ) [Fact (finrank ℝ E = n + 1)]

open scoped ContDiff RealInnerProductSpace

#synth IsManifold (𝓡 n) ω (sphere (0 : E) 1) -- works

but, if my understanding is correct, sphere (0 : E) 1 cannot be given the structure of a Riemannian manifold in the natural way, because 

#synth MetricSpace (sphere (0 : E) 1)

also works, coming from docs#Subtype.metricSpace , and this is the wrong metric. It was suggested that we fix this with

def RoundSphere : Type _ := sphere (0 : E) 1
  deriving TopologicalSpace, ChartedSpace (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)),
  IsManifold (𝓡 n) ω

and this is what we did. Is this RoundSphere definition suitable for Mathlib? If not, do we want to be able to give the sphere a structure of a Riemannian manifold in mathlib, and if so then how? If so, should we refactor the manifold work on the sphere?

If it is OK, how would people feel about this instance?

noncomputable instance : PseudoEMetricSpace (RoundSphere E n) :=
  PseudoEMetricSpace.ofRiemannianMetric (𝓡 n) (RoundSphere E n)

(i.e. give it the metric coming from the Riemannian structure we constructed)? Or should this be local?

2) To make IsRiemannianManifold (𝓡 n) (RoundSphere E n) typecheck, we had to make this instance:

noncomputable instance : IsContinuousRiemannianBundle (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))
      fun (x : RoundSphere E n) ↦ TangentSpace (𝓡 n) x := ...

which we made by proving IsContinuousRiemannianBundle.comap, pulling back a continuous Riemannian bundles from the target to the source of some kind of immersion. Currently we have this under the assumption ∀ x, IsDiffImmersionAt I J f x (there is no global IsDiffImmersion it seems). I am a bit confused about the status of IsDiffImmersionAt. Right now we have docs#Manifold.IsImmersionAt.isDiffImmersionAt , so it seems like IsDiffImmersionAt is more general (I know nothing about infinite-dimensional manifolds) and thus pulling back continuous Riemannian bundles under the DiffImmersion hypothesis is a stronger theorem and thus more appropriate for mathlib. But should we be avoiding this def completely?

(remark: in the application to spheres we use docs#injective_mvfderiv_subtypeVal_sphere and then docs#IsDiffImmersionAt.of_injective_of_finiteDimensional).

3) I was relieved, but also a little surprised, that we never had to do anything about ContMDiff stuff, but should we really be pulling back something stronger than continuous Riemannian bundles?

[Edit: here is the current version of the construction https://gist.github.com/kbuzzard/791b850d81a2bc8430aac6ae2bca3536 but I want to tidy it up before I start making PRs; parts were written by AI but a lot of it is human-generated]

Nice work!
I believe I answered (2) on the PR already. Is there something else you're wondering about?
By the way, #42983 (introduce a IsNormableSpace typeclass) will probably be useful to make this cleanly. Has been awaiting review for two weeks.

I needed the round metric dθ2+sin⁡2θdϕ2d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta d\phi^2dθ2+sin2θdϕ2 for a blog post I am writing and I just did it in coordinates (θ\thetaθ and ϕ\phiϕ) but then I needed a chart which of course one has to prove is a chart. I want an orthonormal frame on my chart (can't be global because of the hairy ball) so although I thought of going the pullback route I actually needed the explicit formula (for my chart: roughly the sphere minus the north and south poles).

Oh yeah, this was just a dump of files because I was doing lots of things at once.

If you want me to use immersions then I think I am missing the fact that the inclusion from the round n-sphere into the n+1-dimensional space is an immersion: right now we know it's injective on tangent spaces by docs#injective_mvfderiv_subtypeVal_sphere and I want to get from this to "it's an immersion" but I'm not sure what the lemma should say.

You want the following lemma, which I'll add to mathlib soon. (There's also a version with boundary, which you won't need.)

import Mathlib

open scoped ContDiff
open Function Manifold

variable {𝕜 M N E E' H H' : Type*} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜]
  [NormedAddCommGroup E]
  [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] [TopologicalSpace H] {I : ModelWithCorners 𝕜 E H} {n : ℕ∞ω} [TopologicalSpace M]
  [ChartedSpace H M] [IsManifold I n M]
  [NormedAddCommGroup E'] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E'] [TopologicalSpace H'] {J : ModelWithCorners 𝕜 E' H'}
  [TopologicalSpace N] [ChartedSpace H' N] [IsManifold J n N]

theorem IsDiffImmersionAt.isImmersionAt_of_boundaryless [BoundarylessManifold I M] {f : M → N} {x : M} (hf : IsDiffImmersionAt I J f x) :
  IsImmersionAt I J n f x := sorry

/-- A map `f : M → N` with injective differential `mfderiv% f x` is an immersion at `x`:
version for `M` having no boundary and `N` being finite-dimensional. -/
lemma IsImmersionAt.of_mfderiv_injective_of_boundaryless
    [BoundarylessManifold I M] [CompleteSpace 𝕜] [FiniteDimensional 𝕜 E']
    {f : M → N} {x : M} (hf : Injective (mfderiv% f x)) : IsImmersionAt I J n f x :=
  (IsDiffImmersionAt.of_injective_of_finiteDimensional hf).isImmersionAt_of_boundaryless

Maybe you also want

/-- A map `f : M → N` with injective differential `mfderiv% f x` is an immersion at `x`:
version for `M` having no boundary and `N` being finite-dimensional. -/
lemma IsImmersion.of_mfderiv_injective_of_boundaryless
    [BoundarylessManifold I M] [CompleteSpace 𝕜] [FiniteDimensional 𝕜 E']
    {f : M → N} (hf : ∀ x, Injective (mfderiv% f x)) : IsImmersion I J n f := sorry

I can look into that at the same time.

Just for fun I proved that this metric is really dθ2+sin⁡2θdϕ2d\theta^2 + \sin^2{\theta}d\phi^2dθ2+sin2θdϕ2 on the longitude / latitude chart (proving this was a chart was surprisingly hard work). No doubt this can be generalised from S2S^2S2 to SnS^nSn: https://github.com/idontgetoutmuch/roundMetric/tree/main
